newsitem.title: USA: Older drivers on anxiety drug in more crashes - study.
newsitem.headline: Older drivers on anxiety drug in more crashes - study.

text.p: Elderly drivers taking the most commonly prescribed drug for anxiety and insomnia are at greater risk of being involved in serious car accidents, Canadian researchers said on Tuesday.

Motorists between the ages of 67 and 84 who were in the first week of treatment with benzodiazepine were 45 percent more likely than non-medicated elderly drivers to be in crashes resulting in injuries, researchers at McGill University and Royal Victoria Hospital in Montreal said.
The risk of accidents remained 26 percent higher even after a year of taking the medication, which can impair motor function and cause drowsiness and confusion.

"The high prevalence of use among the elderly, combined with the increasing number of elderly drivers, makes this an area of particular public health concern," wrote study author Brenda Hemmelgarn in the Journal of the American Medical Association.
The risks of driving while taking short-acting forms of the drug were not examined.
"The studies ... add to the already long list of reasons to avoid benzodiazepines in older patients," Wayne Ray of Vanderbilt University School of Medicine wrote in an accompanying editorial.

He said the study could raise already heightened public concerns about impaired drivers and result in stricter limitations on older drivers who, like many, are reliant on the automobile for their mobility and independence.
